payload.headline: Microsoft falls 2.27% to 506.24 after reported Outlook outage; still a hold

summary.thesis: The business keeps improving: sales growth is speeding up and margins are rising. But heavy spending has cut free cash flow, so the price only makes sense if that spending later turns into cash.
summary.decision: Long-term: hold, and add only at the strongest support zone. Swing: wait for a test of support rather than buying into today's drop.
summary.act_at: Add at 491.22; swing entry 491.22, stop 480.69, target 515.65

payload.happening: Microsoft closed at 506.24, down 2.27% on the day. That puts it at the bottom of its current trading zone (504.96–512.76) and below its 20-day (527.33) and 50-day (519.61) averages. The Verge reported a large Outlook outage today. The next earnings report is due 2027-01-27.
payload.business: Some things change the business itself. Sales grew 18.8% from a year earlier last quarter, up from 18.3% two quarters ago. Operating margin, the share of sales left after running costs, rose to 47.1% from 46.27%. Analysts raised their next-year earnings-per-share estimate by 2.2% over 30 days, to 24.2. The weak spot is cash. Free cash flow is the cash left after running and building the business. It fell to 60.0B over the last twelve months, from 78.0B a year earlier. The filings say each dollar invested now earns 30¢ a year, against 51¢ three years ago, so the heavy spending is not paying back yet. The reported Outlook outage is a reliability and reputation issue. Nothing in the data shows it has hurt demand, margins or cash, so for now it moves sentiment, not the business. The balance sheet is not at risk: Microsoft holds 29.0B in net cash (cash minus debt) and 64.5B in liquidity. What is at risk is whether the spending pays off in cash. Sales and margins are not.

worth.text: The methods disagree a lot. A cash-flow model (DCF) values future free cash flow in today's money. Starting from the current 60.0B of free cash flow, it gives 179.39 (bear), 216.47 (base) and 285.33 (bull), all far below 506.24. To justify today's price, free cash flow would have to start growing at 41.3% a year. That is well above sales growth of 18% last year, 17% over three years, and the 21% earnings growth analysts expect next year. Even at 30% starting growth, the model gives only 337.53. Against its own history, the stock looks fair. Its price-to-sales range gives 475.73 (low), 535.43 (middle) and 592.92 (high). Price-to-sales is 10.9, which sits at the 38th percentile of its own 5-year range. But it is far above the 4.0 median of similar companies. On earnings, the stock trades at 26.4 times trailing earnings and 20.9 times next year's. The gap between the methods comes from one choice: whether today's depressed cash flow or the improving earnings is the right base for valuing the company. I use the own-history range, because earnings and margins are rising while cash flow is held down by spending.
worth.key_assumption: The spending that cut free cash flow from 78.0B to 60.0B turns back into cash. If it does, earnings (next-year EPS estimate 24.2) are the right basis for value, not today's cash flow.

bull: Growth is speeding up, not slowing: quarterly sales grew 18.8% from a year earlier, against 18.3% two quarters ago.
Profitability is improving: operating margin rose to 47.1% from 46.27%, and the next-year EPS estimate rose 2.2% in 30 days to 24.2.
On next year's earnings the stock trades at 20.9 times. Its price-to-sales sits at only the 38th percentile of its own 5-year range.
bear: Free cash flow fell to 60.0B from 78.0B, and each invested dollar now earns 30¢ a year against 51¢ three years ago.
Today's price assumes free cash flow starts growing at 41.3% a year. The base cash-flow value is only 216.47.
Price-to-sales of 10.9 is far above the 4.0 peer median, which leaves little room for a miss. The tech market is also reported to be in a downtrend.

levels.what: Today's close is inside the 475.73–535.43 fair range. That gives no reason to sell, and no margin of safety for new money.
Top of the strongest support zone (486.0–491.22, 8 touches), close to the 475.73 own-history low. This is where adding makes sense.
Middle of the own-history range. Above it the stock is no longer cheap even on its own history, and the case for trimming grows as it nears 592.92.

longterm.why: Sales and margins are improving, but two of three valuation measures lean expensive because cash flow is weak. The reported outage is a sentiment issue and does not change that balance.

swing.why: The price closed near the floor of the 504.96–512.76 zone after a 2.27% drop, below its 20-day and 50-day averages, with no trend. A cleaner setup is a test of the 486.0–491.22 support: entry 491.22, stop 480.69, first target 515.65.

decision.timing: The 2027-01-15 options price a 9.6% move, and that expiry closes before the 2027-01-27 report. So no new long-term money before that report's free cash flow figure, unless the price reaches 486.0–491.22.

change_mind: A close below 486.0, which breaks the 8-touch support: I would stop adding and look to the 472.2–480.69 zone and the 475.73 own-history low.
In the 2027-01-27 report, trailing free cash flow still at or below 60.0B while operating margin stays near 47.1%: that weakens the case for valuing on earnings, and the bias moves toward trim.
A close above 524.43, the top of the first resistance zone, which puts the price back above the 20-day average: that would turn the swing view to enter, targeting 539.37–543.21.
payload.what_changed: Unchanged: still hold, because the drop to 506.24 on a reported Outlook outage left the price inside the 475.73–535.43 fair range and above the 486.0–491.22 support.
